steps.title: Predict the first second
steps.explanation: Start from rest with a constant 4 N horizontal net force on 2 kg. F/m gives 2 m/s², so at 1 s the velocity is 2 m/s and the displacement is ½ × 2 × 1² = 1 m. The grey origin stays fixed; the arrow encodes force, not velocity.
steps.observe: Displacement = 1 m; velocity = 2 m/s. Work 4 × 1 = 4 J equals kinetic energy ½ × 2 × 2² = 4 J.

steps.title: Double time, quadruple distance
steps.explanation: Keep the force and mass fixed and advance the analytic solution to 2 s. Acceleration is unchanged. Velocity grows linearly with time, but displacement grows with time squared. No time-stepping solver or display-speed assumption enters this calculation.
steps.observe: Displacement increases from 1 to 4 m, while velocity increases from 2 to 4 m/s. Work and kinetic energy both become 16 J.

steps.title: Double mass at the same time
steps.explanation: Keep 4 N and 2 s but double the mass to 4 kg. The acceleration halves to 1 m/s². Both displacement and velocity halve relative to the previous state; the change is caused by mass, not an animation setting.
steps.observe: At 2 s, displacement = 2 m and velocity = 2 m/s. Work = kinetic energy = 8 J; the work-minus-kinetic residual is zero.

steps.title: Negative direction can mean positive work
steps.explanation: Return to 2 kg and reverse the force. Acceleration, velocity and displacement all point along negative x. The work is still positive because force and displacement have the same sign: (−4 N)(−4 m) = 16 J.
steps.observe: Displacement = −4 m and velocity = −4 m/s, while work and kinetic energy are both +16 J. A negative force is not by itself negative work.

audit.finding: The embedded adapter fixed time at 1 s and omitted velocity and the independent work/kinetic comparison, so the chapter’s time-scaling example could not be performed.
audit.change: Added a bounded elapsed-time control, origin marker, velocity and work-balance readouts, with four analytic comparisons.
audit.remaining: Constant horizontal force from rest only; no contact, drag, deformation or biological interpretation. Floating-point comparisons are tests, not Lean verification of JavaScript.
